subject: physics
title: Series and parallel circuits
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Series and parallel circuits — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.2.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Series and parallel circuits, specification section 4.2.2.
final_note: You worked through Series and parallel circuits — 19 specification statements.

concepts.term: Series connection
concepts.def: Components are connected in series when they are joined one after another in a single loop, so there is only one path for charge to follow. Every charge that passes through one component must pass through all the others.

concepts.term: Parallel connection
concepts.def: Components are connected in parallel when each one is joined across the same two points, so each component sits on its own branch. There is more than one path for charge to follow between those two points.

concepts.term: Circuits with both series and parallel parts
concepts.def: There are two ways of joining electrical components, in series and in parallel, and some circuits include both. For example, a single resistor joined in series with the cell may supply two further resistors that are joined in parallel with each other. Each part of such a circuit obeys the rule for the way it is joined.

concepts.term: Current in a series circuit
concepts.def: For components connected in series there is the same current through each component. An ammeter placed anywhere in the single loop gives the same reading, because charge is not used up as it passes through a component.

concepts.term: Sharing of potential difference in series
concepts.def: For components connected in series the total potential difference of the power supply is shared between the components. The individual potential differences add up to the supply potential difference, and the largest share is across the component with the largest resistance.

concepts.term: Total resistance in series
concepts.def: For components connected in series the total resistance of two components is the sum of the resistance of each component. Adding a further resistor in series therefore always makes the total resistance larger.

concepts.term: R_total = R_1 + R_2
concepts.def: The equation for two resistors joined in series, given in the specification as R_total = R_1 + R_2. It is one of the equations students are expected to recall and apply, not one that is provided.

concepts.term: Resistance and its unit
concepts.def: Resistance is given the symbol R and is measured in ohms, symbol Ω. Every resistance quoted or calculated in this section, including a total resistance found from R_total = R_1 + R_2, is written with the unit Ω.

concepts.term: Potential difference in a parallel circuit
concepts.def: For components connected in parallel the potential difference across each component is the same. Each branch is joined across the same two points, so each branch has the full supply potential difference across it.

concepts.term: Total current in a parallel circuit
concepts.def: For components connected in parallel the total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components. The current from the supply divides between the branches and recombines, so the branch currents add up to the total.

concepts.term: Total resistance of two resistors in parallel
concepts.def: For two resistors connected in parallel the total resistance is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor. A numerical calculation of this total resistance is not required.

concepts.term: Circuit diagram
concepts.def: A drawing that uses standard circuit symbols and straight connecting lines to show how components are joined. Circuit diagrams are used to construct series and parallel circuits containing a variety of common components, and to check that a circuit that has been built matches the intended one.

concepts.term: Connecting an ammeter
concepts.def: An ammeter measures current and is always connected in series with the component whose current is being measured, so that the same current passes through the meter and the component.

concepts.term: Connecting a voltmeter
concepts.def: A voltmeter measures potential difference and is always connected in parallel across the component, so that the meter and the component have the same potential difference across them.

concepts.term: Why adding resistors in series increases total resistance
concepts.def: In series there is a single path, so charge must pass through every resistor in turn and each one opposes its flow. The oppositions add, so the total resistance rises and, for the same supply potential difference, the current in the circuit falls.

concepts.term: Why adding resistors in parallel decreases total resistance
concepts.def: Each resistor added in parallel provides an extra path for charge, and each branch has the full supply potential difference across it. The total current drawn from the supply therefore increases, which means the total resistance of the combination has fallen below that of the smallest individual resistor.

concepts.term: Equivalent resistance
concepts.def: The resistance of the single resistor that could replace a combination of resistors without changing the current drawn from the supply. For resistors in series the equivalent resistance is found by adding them, R_total = R_1 + R_2, which turns a multi-resistor problem into a single-resistor one.

concepts.term: dc series circuit for measurement and testing
concepts.def: A test circuit in which the component under test, an ammeter and a variable resistor are joined in series with a dc supply, with a voltmeter connected in parallel across the component. Because the components are in series, the ammeter reads exactly the current in the component under test, and the voltmeter reads the potential difference across it alone.

concepts.term: Variable resistor in a test circuit
concepts.def: A resistor whose resistance can be changed. Placed in series, it changes the total resistance of the circuit and so changes the current through every component in the loop, which lets a range of readings be taken from one supply without changing the supply itself.

concepts.term: Using V = I R in series calculations
concepts.def: Calculations of the currents, potential differences and resistances in a dc series circuit use potential difference = current × resistance, V = I R (from section 4.2.1.3), applied together with the series rules: the same current through each component, the supply potential difference shared between the components, and R_total = R_1 + R_2.

concepts.term: Effect of a break in the circuit
concepts.def: A key difference between the two ways of joining components. A series circuit has one path, so a break anywhere in it stops the current everywhere. A parallel circuit has more than one path, so a break in one branch leaves the other branches with a complete path and they keep working.

mcqs.q: A lamp and a resistor are connected in series with a cell. An ammeter between the cell and the lamp reads 0.30 A. A second ammeter is placed between the lamp and the resistor. What does it read?
options: Under 0.30 A, since some of the current is used up inside the lamp
0.30 A, since in series the current through each component is the same
0.15 A, since the current is shared between the lamp and the resistor
It depends on how the resistance of the resistor compares with the lamp
mcqs.explain: For components connected in series there is the same current through each component, so both ammeters read 0.30 A.

mcqs.q: A 6 V battery is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor?
options: 4 V
3 V
6 V
2 V
mcqs.explain: R_total = 2 Ω + 4 Ω = 6 Ω, so the current is 6 V ÷ 6 Ω = 1 A. Across the 4 Ω resistor, V = 1 A × 4 Ω = 4 V.

mcqs.q: A 3 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Which statement about the total resistance of the pair is correct?
options: It is less than 3 Ω, below the smaller of the two resistances
It is 9 Ω, because the two resistances are added together
It is 4.5 Ω, the value halfway between the two resistances
It is 3 Ω, because charge takes the easier of the two paths
mcqs.explain: For two resistors in parallel the total resistance is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.

mcqs.q: A 5 Ω resistor and a 7 Ω resistor are connected in series. What single resistance could replace them without changing the current drawn from the supply?
options: 6 Ω
5 Ω
mcqs.explain: R_total = R_1 + R_2 = 5 Ω + 7 Ω = 12 Ω, the equivalent resistance of the series pair.

mcqs.q: Which equation gives the total resistance of two resistors joined in series?
options: R_total = R_1 − R_2
R_total = R_1 × R_2
R_total = R_1 + R_2
R_total = ½(R_1 + R_2)
mcqs.explain: This is the equation given in the specification for two components in series, and it must be recalled.

mcqs.q: In a dc series circuit the potential difference across one resistor is 12 V and the current through it is 4 A. What is the resistance of this resistor?
options: 3 V
3 A
3 Ω
mcqs.explain: R = V ÷ I = 12 V ÷ 4 A = 3, and the specification gives resistance, R, in ohms, Ω.

mcqs.q: Two lamps are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. What is the potential difference across the lamps?
options: 6 V across each lamp
24 V across each lamp
12 V across lamp 1 only
12 V across each lamp
mcqs.explain: For components connected in parallel the potential difference across each component is the same, and equals the supply potential difference.

mcqs.q: Two resistors are connected in parallel. The current in one branch is 0.4 A and the current in the other branch is 0.6 A. What is the reading on an ammeter in the main circuit, between the battery and the branches?
mcqs.explain: The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components: 0.4 A + 0.6 A.

mcqs.q: A student wants to measure both the current through a resistor and the potential difference across it. How should the two meters be connected?
options: Ammeter in series with the resistor, voltmeter across it
Ammeter across the resistor, voltmeter in series with it
Both meters connected in series with the resistor
Both meters connected in parallel with the resistor
mcqs.explain: An ammeter must carry the current it measures, so it goes in the loop; a voltmeter measures between two points, so it goes across the component.

mcqs.q: Explain why adding a second resistor in series with the first increases the total resistance of the circuit.
options: The extra resistor creates a second path, so the charge is held back more strongly
The first resistor uses up some of the current, leaving less to push round the loop
There is one path, so charge passes through both resistors and the opposition adds
Adding any component to a circuit always increases its total resistance
mcqs.explain: In series the single path runs through every resistor in turn, so the resistances add and the current falls for the same supply potential difference.

mcqs.q: Explain why adding a second resistor in parallel with the first decreases the total resistance of the circuit.
options: The two resistors share the current, so each of them has less work to do than before
Adding a resistor must add resistance, so the total is larger than either of them
The extra branch is another path for charge, so more current is drawn from the supply
The total is the average of the two resistances, so it lies between the two values
mcqs.explain: Each branch has the full supply potential difference across it, so a second branch increases the total current, which means the total resistance has fallen.

mcqs.q: A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor. What is the current in the circuit?
mcqs.explain: R_total = 4 Ω + 8 Ω = 12 Ω, so I = V ÷ R = 12 V ÷ 12 Ω = 1.0 A.

mcqs.q: A 6 Ω resistor and a 9 Ω resistor are connected in series with a 30 V supply. Using the equivalent resistance of the pair, what is the current in the circuit?
mcqs.explain: The equivalent resistance is R_total = 6 Ω + 9 Ω = 15 Ω, so I = V ÷ R = 30 V ÷ 15 Ω = 2.0 A.

mcqs.q: A resistor is tested using a dc circuit in which the resistor, an ammeter and a variable resistor are joined in series, with a voltmeter across the resistor. Why is this a good design for the test?
options: The variable resistor alters the potential difference of the supply, so several values can be tested
The ammeter reads the current in the resistor itself, and the variable resistor changes it
The ammeter is kept in parallel, so it does not change the current in the resistor under test
The series connection puts the full potential difference of the supply across the fixed resistor
mcqs.explain: In series there is the same current through each component, so the ammeter reading is the current in the resistor under test, while the variable resistor alters the total resistance to give a range of readings.

mcqs.q: In the series test circuit above, the resistance of the variable resistor is increased. What happens to the current through the component under test?
options: It rises, because a larger resistance gives the charges a bigger push round
It falls, because the total resistance of the series circuit is now larger
It is unchanged, because the current in a series circuit is always the same
Only the current in the variable resistor falls, and the rest is unaffected
mcqs.explain: R_total has increased, so for the same supply potential difference the current in the single loop is smaller.

mcqs.q: Two lamps are lit by one battery. One lamp is unscrewed from its holder and the other stays lit at the same brightness. What does this show?
options: They are in series: the current simply carries on round the rest of the single loop
They are in parallel, so the remaining lamp now takes the share of the one removed
They are in parallel: the remaining lamp still has a complete path and the same potential difference
They are in parallel, so the current drawn from the battery is exactly the same
mcqs.explain: A parallel circuit has more than one path, and each branch has the supply potential difference across it, so removing one branch leaves the other unchanged.

mcqs.q: A circuit diagram shows a cell, a switch and two identical lamps drawn one after another in a single loop. Which statement is correct when the switch is closed?
options: Both light, but the lamp nearer the positive terminal is brighter
Both light, with the full potential difference of the cell across each
Both light, and the current divides equally between the two lamps
Both lamps light, with the same current through each of them
mcqs.explain: The lamps are in series, and for components connected in series there is the same current through each component.

mcqs.q: A 9 V supply is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 7 Ω resistor. Which statement about the potential differences is correct?
options: 4.5 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 4.5 V across the 7 Ω resistor
9 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 9 V across the 7 Ω resistor
7 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 2 V across the 7 Ω resistor
2 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 7 V across the 7 Ω resistor
mcqs.explain: The current is 9 V ÷ 9 Ω = 1 A, so V = 1 A × 2 Ω = 2 V and V = 1 A × 7 Ω = 7 V, and these add to the 9 V supply.

mcqs.q: A 4 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Which of these values could be the total resistance of the pair?
options: 8 Ω
4 Ω
3 Ω
mcqs.explain: The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor, so it must be below 4 Ω. Only this value is.

mcqs.q: A resistor is connected in series with a battery, and this resistor supplies two further resistors that are connected in parallel with each other. Which statement about this circuit is correct?
options: The current in the series resistor equals the sum of the two branch currents
The current in the series resistor equals the current in each of the branches
The potential difference of the battery is shared equally by all three resistors
The potential difference across the series resistor is the same as the supply
mcqs.explain: The series resistor carries the whole circuit current, and the total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components in parallel.
